paragraphs.text: Mitochondrial myopathy with lactic acidosis is an autosomal recessive mitochondrial disorder. Saunders et al. (2015) first described it in a girl with progressive muscle weakness, hypotonia, seizures, poor weight gain, and lactic acidosis who had biallelic loss-of-function PNPLA8 mutations. Later reports widened the phenotype. Abdel-Hamid et al. (2024) recognized congenital-onset, infantile-onset, childhood-onset, and adult-onset forms. Nakamura et al. (2024) reviewed 25 affected individuals and concluded that PNPLA8-related neurologic disease forms a continuum. At one end is developmental and/or degenerative epileptic-dyskinetic encephalopathy with congenital microcephaly and pontocerebellar hypoplasia. At the other is childhood- or later-onset neurodegeneration with ataxia and progressive cerebellar atrophy.

paragraphs.text: Mastaglia et al. (1980) described a 23-year-old man with a mitochondrial myopathy. Twenty-two years before the skeletal myopathy appeared, he had a high-output circulatory state and cardiomyopathy that caused cardiac insufficiency. His venous lactate levels were elevated, and at one stage of the illness he developed severe lactic acidosis. Electron microscopy of muscle showed various mitochondrial abnormalities and an accumulation of neutral lipids, which histochemistry and thin-layer chromatography confirmed. The metabolic defect was not defined.

paragraphs.text: Saunders et al. (2015) reported a 7-year-old girl who was evaluated for a suspected mitochondrial myopathy with dystonia, abnormal gait, and an abnormal muscle biopsy. She was born at term weighing 3.1 kg. She had no symptoms in the first year and met all developmental milestones, although her parents noticed toe-walking. At age 2 she had a positive Gowers sign, and by age 3 years she could no longer walk. She could sit independently for only 10 minutes because of fatigue. Her fine motor skills declined and her speech became dysarthric. She had proximal muscle weakness, tight heel cords, and generalized mildly increased tone. The weakness and dysmetria progressed, and hypotonicity progressed to spasticity of opposing muscle groups. She later developed complex partial seizures with recurrent left temporal lobe spikes on EEG. She had a very lean body habitus and significant lactic acidosis that required bicarbonate supplementation. Brain MRI at 33 months showed subtle increased signal in the medial globus pallidus bilaterally. This finding was no longer seen 2 years later, which the authors suggested reflected maturation of myelination. MR spectroscopy and head CT were normal. A right quadriceps biopsy at age 4 years showed variable fiber size with isolated small atrophic fibers of all subtypes and no ragged red fibers. Electron microscopy showed mitochondria with marked disarray of cristae and globular dense osmiophilic inclusions. It also showed subsarcolemmal aggregates of abnormal mitochondria with concentric lamellar membranes, suggestive of degenerating mitochondria, and increased secondary lysosomes containing residual bodies that appeared to derive from mitochondria.

paragraphs.text: Patient 2 of Shukla et al. (2018), of Indian/Fijian origin and born to nonconsanguineous parents, developed normally until about 13 months of age. She then regressed, with episodes of epilepsia partialis continua and difficult-to-control focal seizures. At 2 years she was nonverbal and needed a gastrostomy tube. Her head growth stopped after age 3 years, and at 15 years her head circumference was 49 cm (-4.7 SD). She had central hypotonia with muscle weakness, choreiform movements, dystonia, proximal muscle weakness, absent muscle stretch reflexes, and severe contractures. Over a decade, brain MRI showed volume loss in the cerebellum, brainstem, and parietal and occipital lobes, with thinning of the corpus callosum. MR spectroscopy showed a persistently elevated lipid-lactate peak. On electron microscopy, muscle biopsy showed enlarged, irregularly shaped mitochondria with surrounding membrane whorls and disrupted cristae, together with electron-dense deposits, lipid droplets, and glycogen pools. Other findings were reduced visual evoked potentials, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with subaortic stenosis, obstructive sleep apnea, and restrictive lung disease.

paragraphs.text: Burnyte et al. (2023) reported 2 adult sibs, a brother and a sister, whose symptoms began at age 14 years. Both had slowly progressive ataxia and sensorimotor polyneuropathy, and their cognition was preserved. The brother, now 49 years old, first developed weakness and distal muscle atrophy of the lower limbs, with ataxia and gait disturbance. He could not walk without assistance from age 17 years. At 30 years he had marked axial ataxia, tetraparesis, decreased muscle tone, wasting of the calves and feet, absent lower-limb reflexes, foot deformities, bilateral Babinski signs, dysmetria, and mild length-dependent hypoesthesia. Nerve conduction studies showed sensorimotor axonal polyneuropathy. He became nonambulant at age 44. At 45 years he had mild dysarthria and horizontal nystagmus, and his Mini-Mental State Examination score was 30/30. Brain MRI showed mild cerebellar atrophy. His sister developed difficulty walking and weakness of both lower limbs at age 14 years. At 21 years she had distal atrophy of all limbs, absent lower-limb reflexes, bilateral Babinski signs, severe axial ataxia, and appendicular dysmetria, and she could not maintain an upright posture. Her cognition was normal, and EMG showed no myopathic changes. Neither sib had visual, auditory, cardiac, or liver dysfunction. Their disease advanced markedly in the teens but progressed only slightly through adulthood.

paragraphs.text: Nakamura et al. (2024) reported 14 individuals (6 male and 8 female) from 12 unrelated families of various origins, many of them consanguineous. Ages at last assessment ranged from 3 days to 33 years. Frequent features were central hypotonia (13 of 13), dystonia (8 of 12), seizures (10 of 14), and cerebellar atrophy (12 of 12). Eight patients (Families 1-8) had severe disease. In this group, features included congenital microcephaly (5 of 7), global developmental delay with no milestones attained (7 of 7), peripheral spasticity (7 of 8), and seizure onset within 7 months of age (8 of 8). Neuroimaging in this group showed a simplified gyral pattern (6 of 6), pontocerebellar hypoplasia (7 of 7), and severe progressive cerebral cortical atrophy (5 of 5). Four patients (Families 11-12) had relatively mild disease. All 4 learned to walk and later had regression of milestones. Three of the 4 had ataxia and 3 had mild or no intellectual disability, and seizures were isolated or absent. Their brain MRI showed little or no cerebral cortical volume loss but progressive cerebellar atrophy. Patients from Families 9 and 10 were of intermediate severity. Nakamura et al. (2024) also identified 2 individuals with biallelic PNPLA8 variants in a non-neurologic cohort. One had optic atrophy and the other had nonsyndromic hearing loss.

paragraphs.text: Nakamura et al. (2024) studied 14 patients from 12 families by exome or genome sequencing with Sanger segregation analysis. They identified 14 PNPLA8 variants, 12 of them novel. Twelve of the 14 patients carried combinations of nonsense, frameshift, and splice-site variants. In patient lymphoblastoid cells, the c.1625+3_1625+6del variant in Patient 1 caused skipping of exons 6 to 8, and his fibroblasts showed a significant reduction in the 77-kDa PNPLA8 protein. Fibroblasts from Patient 6, who carried p.Glu296Lysfs*6, also showed a null effect. SpliceAI predicted that the c.2075-2A-G and c.1684-2A-G variants would abolish splice acceptor sites. Two Iranian individuals from a non-neurologic cohort, one with optic atrophy and one with hearing loss, were homozygous for N-terminal frameshift variants affecting only the 88-kDa isoform. In the optic atrophy family, an affected sib was heterozygous, and the authors considered these variants of undetermined significance.

paragraphs.text: Nakamura et al. (2024) analyzed 25 affected individuals from 20 families. Patients with a relatively mild phenotype and late-onset movement disorders all had biallelic C-terminal frameshift variants (p.Thr757Glnfs*10 or p.Leu759Alafs*4). In contrast, fibroblasts from a severely affected patient homozygous for the missense variant p.Val520Asp showed protein expression similar to controls. The authors concluded that biallelic loss-of-function variants affecting the 77- and 74-kDa isoforms are sufficient for the severe phenotype.
